lesson.title: Docker images layers build cache and multi-stage builds
lesson.why: A container image's construction affects rebuild time, size and exposure. Copying a secret and deleting it later can leave it in an earlier layer, while copying frequently changed source too early can invalidate expensive dependency work.
lesson.what: Docker builds an image from instructions and a build context. Layers capture filesystem changes, cache keys determine reuse and multi-stage builds copy selected artifacts into a smaller runtime stage without carrying every build tool forward.

concepts.name: Layers and deletion
concepts.body: An image combines filesystem layers with configuration. Deleting a file in a later layer hides it in the merged view but does not necessarily remove bytes from earlier layers. Keep credentials out of the build context and use supported ephemeral secret mechanisms.

concepts.name: Cache dependencies
concepts.body: Cache reuse depends on the instruction and relevant inputs, not merely whether a file's name stayed the same. Place relatively stable dependency manifests before frequently changing application source when that matches the build process. A cache hit is not fresh dependency verification.

concepts.name: Context control
concepts.body: The build context defines files available to copy and can accidentally include local configuration or large unrelated directories. A .dockerignore file reduces that exposure and transfer. Excluding a required source file can also make builds fail, so review it with the Dockerfile.

concepts.name: Stage boundaries
concepts.body: A multi-stage build starts separate stages with FROM and copies only necessary outputs into the final stage. Runtime libraries may still be required by a compiled binary. A smaller image is useful but must retain certificates, users and files the application genuinely needs.

e2e: Select and constrain the build context before sending it to the builder.
Evaluate instructions and reuse cache only when the relevant inputs match.
Compile or assemble artifacts in the build stage and copy required outputs forward.
Inspect the final runtime contents and test startup without assuming size alone proves correctness.

tasks.name: Predict cache invalidation
steps: Offline, compare copying the entire application before dependency installation with copying only dependency manifests first. If only a source file changes, the second layout can reuse dependency work. Explain which later steps still need rebuilding and why manifests must accurately describe dependencies.

tasks.name: Calculate final-stage size
tasks.goal: Separate build tools from runtime files.
steps: Assume a builder has 700 MB of tools and produces a 20 MB binary; the runtime base is 10 MB. Copying only that binary yields approximately 30 MB before other required files, not 730 MB. Mark these as hypothetical uncompressed sizes.

tasks.name: Find a layer secret mistake
steps: Review a fictional sequence COPY credential.txt followed by RUN deleting it. Reject the claim that deletion guarantees removal from image history. Propose excluding the file entirely and using an approved ephemeral build-secret interface without creating an actual credential.

tasks.name: Review runtime dependencies
tasks.goal: Prevent a tiny but broken image.
steps: A dynamically linked binary is copied into an empty runtime stage and cannot find its loader. Identify the missing runtime dependency. Compare static linking where appropriate with a minimal compatible runtime base; test requirements rather than blindly choosing the smallest image.

key_terms: Layer: filesystem change set in an image.
Build context: files available to the builder.
Cache key: identity controlling build-step reuse.
Stage: independent build phase beginning with FROM.
lesson.safety: Use offline build reviews only. Do not include secrets, pull unapproved images or send private source to remote builders.
cleanup: Retain the fictional Dockerfile ordering and size worksheet; no images or build caches were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical image shrank after a multi-stage change but no longer starts. What would you inspect?
interview_points: Check copied artifacts, entrypoint and architecture.
Identify dynamic libraries and loader requirements.
Verify runtime certificates, user and filesystem needs.
Do not equate a smaller image with a validated runtime.

containers/docker-images-layers-build-ca.core: Constrain context, keep secrets out of layers and order stable build inputs before volatile source. Multi-stage builds copy required artifacts, not every tool, but must preserve runtime libraries and configuration needed for startup.
objectives: Explain multi-stage size and runtime dependency trade-offs.
prerequisites: Understand files, dependencies and basic Dockerfile instructions.

storyboard.title: A small runtime image still needs its loader
storyboard.objective: Trace artifacts across a multi-stage boundary.

scenes.title: Build artifact produced
scenes.caption: Compilation tools remain in the build stage.
scenes.narration: The build stage compiles the application, then copies its output into a smaller runtime stage without transferring every compiler tool.

scenes.title: Loader is missing
scenes.caption: The binary is not necessarily self-contained.
scenes.narration: The application is dynamically linked. Its runtime stage lacks the required loader, so the entrypoint cannot execute despite a successful build.

scenes.title: Include verified runtime requirements
scenes.caption: Select compatible libraries or a suitable static artifact.
scenes.narration: The image includes the documented runtime dependencies and startup is tested, preserving a small image without sacrificing required execution support.

lesson.title: Container runtime namespaces cgroups and isolation
lesson.why: Containers isolate processes but usually share the host kernel. Knowing which mechanism controls visibility, identity and resource consumption prevents treating a container as an unrestricted miniature virtual machine or a complete security boundary by itself.
lesson.what: A container runtime configures namespaces, control groups, filesystem mounts and process execution. Namespaces create scoped views, cgroups account for and limit resources, and additional kernel security mechanisms constrain what processes may do.

concepts.name: Namespace views
concepts.body: PID, mount, network and other namespaces provide different views of system resources. A process can appear as PID one inside its container while having another host PID. Namespaces reduce visibility but do not create a separate kernel for each container.

concepts.name: Resource controls
concepts.body: Cgroups organize processes for accounting and resource control. CPU quotas bound available execution over time; memory limits can trigger reclaim or termination. A limit is not always a reservation, so scheduling and capacity planning remain separate operational concerns.

concepts.name: Privilege mechanisms
concepts.body: Capabilities divide some privileged operations into smaller grants. Seccomp restricts system calls, while mandatory access controls add policy enforcement. Running without root helps, but privileged flags, host mounts or broad capabilities can weaken isolation regardless of the process username.

concepts.name: Runtime lifecycle
concepts.body: The runtime prepares the environment and starts the container's main process. Signal forwarding and child reaping matter for PID one. When the main process exits, the container normally stops even if the operator expected it to behave like a continuously managed VM.

e2e: The runtime prepares namespace views, mounts and resource-control membership.
It applies identity and security restrictions before starting the main process.
Application work executes against the shared kernel within the configured boundaries.
Resource or lifecycle events affect the process, and the supervisor records exit or restart behavior.

tasks.name: Map isolation mechanisms
tasks.goal: Assign each boundary to its purpose.
steps: On paper, pair process visibility with PID namespaces, network interfaces with network namespaces and memory accounting with cgroups. Explain why a cgroup memory limit does not create a separate kernel or grant permission to access another container's files.

tasks.name: Calculate a CPU quota
steps: A hypothetical cgroup permits 50 milliseconds of CPU time per 100-millisecond period. This represents half a CPU of quota over that interval. Explain that short bursts and throttling can still affect latency, and the quota is not a promise of a dedicated core.

tasks.name: Review a weakened boundary
steps: A fictional container runs as a nonroot user but mounts the host's runtime control socket. Identify that powerful control channel as a major boundary risk. Remove it from the proposed design rather than assuming the nonroot username makes every mounted interface safe.

tasks.name: Plan graceful process exit
steps: Draw a wrapper shell and its application child. Specify signal forwarding and child reaping, or a supported minimal init arrangement. Explain why terminating the wrapper without forwarding a graceful signal can prevent the application from flushing its own work.

key_terms: Namespace: scoped view of kernel resources.
Cgroup: process resource accounting and control group.
Capability: subdivided privileged-operation permission.
PID one: first process in a PID namespace.
lesson.safety: Use offline diagrams. Do not run privileged containers, mount host control sockets or change kernel and cgroup settings.
cleanup: No containers or namespaces were created; keep only the mechanism map.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical team says containers provide the same kernel isolation as VMs. How would you explain the difference?
interview_points: Containers commonly share the host kernel.
Namespaces scope views and cgroups control resources.
Capabilities, seccomp and mounts affect the security boundary.
VMs ordinarily run separate guest kernels behind virtualization.

containers/container-runtime-namespaces-.core: Namespaces isolate views; cgroups control resource consumption; neither creates a separate guest kernel. Review privileges, mounts and syscall restrictions. The container's main process governs lifecycle and must handle signals and child cleanup correctly.
objectives: Distinguish namespaces, cgroups and privilege controls.
Calculate a CPU quota and explain lifecycle behavior.
prerequisites: Understand Linux processes, kernels and resource limits.

storyboard.title: Visibility isolation does not reserve CPU
storyboard.objective: Separate namespace views from cgroup enforcement.

scenes.title: Scoped execution
scenes.caption: The process sees its container view of shared-kernel resources.
scenes.narration: Namespaces provide the process with a scoped view, while its execution still depends on the host kernel and physical resources.

scenes.title: Quota is exhausted
scenes.caption: Resource throttling differs from a visibility failure.
scenes.narration: The process consumes its CPU quota and waits for more scheduling allowance. Its namespace remains intact while latency increases.

scenes.title: Diagnose the correct mechanism
scenes.caption: Inspect resource demand without weakening isolation.
scenes.narration: The operator checks quota and workload demand rather than granting privileges or removing namespace boundaries to address a capacity problem.

lesson.title: Container networking DNS and port publishing
lesson.why: A container's localhost usually means that container, not a neighboring service or the host. Understanding network scope and explicit publishing prevents both failed local integrations and accidentally exposing a development service to other machines.
lesson.what: Container networks connect endpoints within configured scopes. On Docker user-defined networks, embedded DNS supports service-name resolution. Publishing maps a host endpoint to a container endpoint; it is separate from image documentation such as EXPOSE.

concepts.name: Network namespaces
concepts.body: Each isolated network namespace has its own loopback, interfaces and routes. An application connecting to localhost inside a container normally reaches that same namespace. Host-network modes alter this boundary and should not be assumed or enabled as a quick fix.

concepts.name: Service-name resolution
concepts.body: Containers on suitable shared user-defined networks can resolve configured container or service names. IP addresses may change on replacement, so stable names are preferable. Name resolution still does not guarantee the target listens or accepts the requested protocol.

concepts.name: Publishing semantics
concepts.body: EXPOSE documents an intended container port but does not itself publish it on the host. A published mapping chooses host address, host port and container port. Bind the host side to 127.0.0.1 for an intentionally local-only development endpoint.

concepts.name: Two bind boundaries
concepts.body: A process listening only on container loopback may not accept traffic forwarded to its container interface. The application bind inside the container and the published host bind are separate decisions. Validate both while keeping the external host exposure restricted.

e2e: A client resolves a service name within its configured network scope.
It selects the target container port or a deliberately published host endpoint.
Docker networking forwards traffic to the container interface and listening application.
The response follows the connection path; diagnose DNS, publishing and application bind separately.

tasks.name: Predict localhost behavior
steps: Offline, place API and database in separate network namespaces. API connects to localhost:5432. Expected destination is the API's own loopback, not the database. Replace the design with the database's service name on their approved shared network.

tasks.name: Decode a local mapping
steps: Review `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` without running a container. It maps host loopback port 8080 to container port 80. State that EXPOSE 80 alone creates no equivalent host listener and that broad host binding is unnecessary for this exercise.

tasks.name: Diagnose a double-bind mistake
steps: A hypothetical mapping targets container port 80, but the application listens only on 127.0.0.1 inside that container. Identify why forwarding to its container interface can fail. Keep host publishing loopback-only while correcting the internal listener deliberately.

tasks.name: Plan service replacement
tasks.goal: Use stable discovery rather than fixed addresses.
steps: A recreated database changes container IP but retains its Compose service name. Explain why clients must resolve or reconnect through the name rather than hard-code the old IP. Define bounded retries and readiness checks without publishing the database to the host.

key_terms: Publish: map a host endpoint to a container port.
EXPOSE: image metadata documenting a port.
Bridge network: software network connecting container endpoints.
Loopback: address referring to the current network namespace.
lesson.safety: Use command review and paper diagrams; if later testing locally, bind published ports only to loopback and never expose a database by default.
cleanup: No networks or containers were created; future demos must remove only their named project network and containers.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical container has EXPOSE 80 but cannot be reached on host port 8080. What would you inspect?
interview_points: EXPOSE is metadata, not a published mapping.
Check host address and port mapping.
Check the application's internal bind and target port.
Avoid solving local access by exposing every interface.

containers/container-networking-dns-and-.core: Container localhost is namespace-local. Use service DNS on shared networks, not fixed container IPs. EXPOSE does not publish; host binding and internal application binding are separate. Keep development publishing explicitly loopback-only.
objectives: Decode port publishing and internal listener behavior.
prerequisites: Understand IP addresses, ports and network namespaces.

storyboard.title: Host publishing cannot repair container loopback binding
storyboard.objective: Trace the two independent listener boundaries.

scenes.title: Explicit local publishing
scenes.caption: The host endpoint is intentionally loopback-only.
scenes.narration: The host client uses port eight thousand eighty, and the mapping forwards toward container port eighty without exposing other host interfaces.

scenes.title: Internal listener mismatch
scenes.caption: Container loopback is not its network interface.
scenes.narration: The application listens only on its own loopback address, so traffic forwarded to the container interface does not reach that listener.

scenes.title: Correct the internal bind
scenes.caption: Keep the host boundary local while fixing the application path.
scenes.narration: The application binds appropriately inside its namespace, while host publishing remains restricted to loopback and the local request is verified.

lesson.title: Container storage volumes and data persistence
lesson.why: A container can be replaced while its data survives, or removed together with data unintentionally. Distinguishing writable layers, named volumes and host bind mounts is essential before deciding how to back up or clean up an application.
lesson.what: Container images provide initial filesystem content, while running containers add a writable layer. Volumes and bind mounts attach external storage at chosen paths. Their lifecycle, ownership and backup needs are separate from the container's process lifecycle.

concepts.name: Writable-layer limits
concepts.body: Files written only into a container's writable layer usually disappear when that container is removed. Restarting the same container is not the same as recreating it. Do not treat observed persistence across one restart as proof of durable storage design.

concepts.name: Named volumes
concepts.body: Docker-managed volumes persist independently of individual container replacement unless explicitly removed. Multiple containers can access a volume, but the application must support concurrent writers. A volume preserves bytes; it does not automatically provide consistent backups or replication.

concepts.name: Bind mounts
concepts.body: Bind mounts expose a specific host path inside the container. They are useful for development but couple deployment to host layout and permissions. Writable mounts can modify host files, so avoid sensitive directories and use read-only access where the workload permits.

concepts.name: Mount masking and ownership
concepts.body: A mount at a container path hides image content there while mounted. User IDs and permissions determine access to mounted data; a name inside the image does not automatically match host ownership. Plan initialization and migration without recursively changing unrelated host permissions.

e2e: Identify which application paths contain durable state versus disposable scratch data.
Attach an appropriate volume or tightly scoped bind mount with explicit access mode.
Write data and verify persistence across the intended replacement lifecycle.
Back up consistently, test restoration and remove storage only after its retention decision is explicit.

tasks.name: Predict persistence
steps: Offline, put file A in the writable layer and file B in a named volume. Restarting the same container can retain both; removing and recreating the container loses A but can retain B when the same volume is attached.

tasks.name: Calculate storage growth
steps: A fictional volume receives 200 MB per day and retains 30 days. Raw retained data is 6,000 MB before indexes, replication or overhead. Explain why deleting old containers does not automatically release this independently retained volume data.

tasks.name: Review a bind mount
steps: Compare mounting a disposable project input directory read-only with mounting the host home directory writable. Select the narrow input mount and document required files. Reject the broad mount even if it would make a missing-file error disappear.

tasks.name: Design a restore rehearsal
tasks.goal: Test useful recovery rather than copied bytes.
steps: A fictional database volume is backed up while writes occur. Ask whether its backup method provides application consistency. Plan restoration into a separate empty demo volume and verify record integrity before considering the backup usable; do not copy a live production volume.

key_terms: Writable layer: container-specific filesystem changes.
Named volume: independently managed persistent storage.
Bind mount: host-path attachment.
Mount point: path where attached storage becomes visible.
lesson.safety: Use offline scenarios only. Do not mount host home or system paths, delete volumes, or change ownership recursively.
cleanup: No storage was created; any later demo cleanup must name its exact volume and require an explicit data-retention decision.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical database survives container restarts but loses data after recreation. What storage assumption was wrong?
interview_points: Inspect whether data lived only in the writable layer.
Distinguish restart from remove-and-create.
Attach persistent storage to the actual database data path.
Verify backups and cleanup ownership separately from container lifecycle.

containers/container-storage-volumes-and.core: Writable layers, named volumes and bind mounts have different lifecycles. A restart is not recreation. Keep durable data on deliberately managed storage, constrain host mounts and test consistent restoration before calling a backup reliable.
objectives: Predict data survival across container lifecycle events.
Design scoped mounts and recovery verification.
prerequisites: Understand filesystem paths and container replacement.

storyboard.title: Recreation removes the writable layer, not the named volume
storyboard.objective: Explain independent process and storage lifecycles.

scenes.title: Two write locations
scenes.caption: Only the intended data path uses external storage.
scenes.narration: The application writes scratch files to its layer and durable records to a named volume attached at the configured data path.

scenes.title: Container removed
scenes.caption: Its writable layer is not a durable recovery source.
scenes.narration: Removal discards the container's writable layer. The named volume remains unless a separate storage-removal action explicitly deletes it.

scenes.title: Attach and verify
scenes.caption: The replacement uses the same retained data volume.
scenes.narration: A replacement attaches the retained volume and verifies application data, while backup and eventual deletion remain separate controlled decisions.

lesson.title: Container registries image tags and provenance
lesson.why: Two machines can pull the same tag at different times and receive different bytes. Reliable promotion requires identifying exact image content and its build origin, not assuming that a familiar tag proves review, freshness or safety.
lesson.what: A registry stores image manifests and referenced blobs. Tags are human-friendly references that may move; digests identify content. Provenance and attestations connect artifacts to build inputs and processes under a verification policy.

concepts.name: Tags and digests
concepts.body: A tag such as stable is a mutable reference unless registry policy prevents updates. A digest identifies a particular manifest's content. Pinning a digest improves identity stability but does not patch the image automatically or prove its publisher is trustworthy.

concepts.name: Multi-platform manifests
concepts.body: An image index can refer to separate manifests for different architectures or operating systems. A client selects a compatible platform. Record whether the pinned digest identifies the index or one platform image, and test the platforms actually deployed.

concepts.name: Promotion and access
concepts.body: Promote a verified artifact rather than rebuilding independently in each environment. Registry read and write permissions are separate concerns; broad push permission can replace trusted tags. Retention policies must preserve artifacts needed for rollback and investigation.

concepts.name: Provenance verification
concepts.body: Build provenance can describe source revision, builder identity and parameters. Verification must check expected identities and predicates, not merely that an attestation exists. An attacker can attach metadata to an untrusted build, so evidence needs a meaningful trust policy.

e2e: The builder produces image content and records source and build evidence.
The registry stores manifests and blobs, with tags pointing to selected content.
Deployment resolves or pins the approved digest and verifies required provenance.
Promotion and rollback reuse retained verified content while access and retention policies preserve identity.

tasks.name: Track a moving tag
steps: Offline, stable points to digest D1 on Monday and D2 on Tuesday. Two fresh pulls by tag can differ; two pulls pinned to D1 identify the same manifest content. D1 and D2 are diagram labels, not real digest strings.

tasks.name: Reason about platform selection
tasks.goal: Distinguish an index from its images.
steps: Draw one image index pointing to amd64 and arm64 manifests. Explain why successful testing on amd64 does not establish arm64 runtime behavior, even when both are published under one tag. Record platform-specific verification in the release plan.

tasks.name: Define a promotion record
steps: Create a fictional record containing source commit label C1, image digest label D1, builder identity and approved test evidence fields. Mark evidence pending rather than inventing a pass. Promote the same artifact identity instead of rebuilding separately for production.

tasks.name: Review registry permissions
steps: A deployment reader also has permission to overwrite release tags. Remove that write ability from the proposed role and assign publishing to a controlled build identity. Include retention for the last known-good digest so a cleanup policy cannot silently remove rollback material.

key_terms: Registry: image manifest and blob store.
Digest: content-derived artifact identifier.
Image index: multi-platform manifest collection.
Provenance: evidence describing artifact production.
lesson.safety: Use symbolic identities only. Do not log into registries, push tags, pull private images or publish invented attestations.
cleanup: Retain the promotion template with pending evidence; no registry content or credentials were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical deployment using the same image tag behaves differently across two environments. What would you compare?
interview_points: Resolve exact manifest digests and platforms.
Check whether the tag moved or environments rebuilt separately.
Verify expected builder and source provenance.
Compare runtime configuration without assuming the tag guarantees identical bytes.

containers/container-registries-image-ta.core: Tags may move; digests identify content but do not prove safety. Distinguish multi-platform indexes from platform images. Promote verified artifacts with source/builder evidence and protect registry publishing and rollback retention.
objectives: Explain tag, digest and platform identity.
Design a trustworthy artifact promotion record.
prerequisites: Understand container images and release artifacts.

storyboard.title: One tag points to different content over time
storyboard.objective: Explain immutable artifact selection during promotion.

scenes.title: Tag resolves to D1
scenes.caption: The first environment receives one manifest identity.
scenes.narration: The deployment resolves stable to the first manifest. The tag is a name, while the digest identifies the chosen content.

scenes.title: Tag moves to D2
scenes.caption: A later pull can receive different content under the same name.
scenes.narration: The publisher changes stable. A second environment now obtains another manifest despite using identical tag text in its configuration.

scenes.title: Promote a verified digest
scenes.caption: Pin identity and verify expected build evidence.
scenes.narration: The release process selects the approved digest and platform, checks provenance and retains that content for consistent promotion and rollback.

lesson.title: Container security rootless builds and scanning
lesson.why: A vulnerability report is only one part of container risk. Rootless operation, restricted mounts and small privilege sets reduce consequences, while scanning identifies known issues that still require context, remediation and verification.
lesson.what: Container hardening addresses both build and runtime boundaries. Rootless Docker runs daemon and containers without host root privileges using user namespaces. Running a nonroot process inside a rootful runtime is helpful but is not the same configuration.

concepts.name: Rootless versus nonroot
concepts.body: Rootless mode changes daemon and container privilege on the host. A Dockerfile USER instruction changes the process identity inside the container but does not make a rootful daemon rootless. Both need supported user mappings, permissions and documented operational limitations.

concepts.name: Least runtime privilege
concepts.body: Drop unnecessary capabilities, avoid privileged mode and sensitive host mounts, and use appropriate seccomp or mandatory-access policies. Read-only root filesystems reduce writable surface but applications may need explicitly scoped scratch space. No single flag substitutes for threat-specific review.

concepts.name: Scanning limitations
concepts.body: Image scanners match detected components against vulnerability intelligence. Results depend on package detection, advisory freshness and distribution backports. A clean report does not prove absence of vulnerabilities; a finding needs affected-version and reachability context without dismissing severity arbitrarily.

concepts.name: Build supply chain
concepts.body: Use reviewed base images, controlled dependencies and build secrets that do not enter layers. Build provenance and digest identity connect scanned content to deployed content. Scanning one tag then deploying a changed tag breaks that evidence chain.

e2e: Select a trusted base and build without embedding secrets or unnecessary tools.
Scan the resulting immutable artifact and triage findings against actual component versions.
Deploy that same artifact with least privilege and bounded writable paths.
Monitor runtime behavior and update dependencies through a verified rebuild and rollout process.

tasks.name: Compare privilege configurations
steps: Offline, compare a nonroot USER in a container managed by a rootful daemon with a rootless daemon running containers. State which host privilege boundary changes in each case. Do not install runtimes or edit user mappings for this exercise.

tasks.name: Calculate remediation coverage
steps: A fictional scan has ten applicable findings, six fixed by a rebuilt base and two proven not affected through vendor evidence. Two remain unresolved. Report eight dispositions and two open findings, not a claim that the image is vulnerability-free.

tasks.name: Design a writable-path policy
steps: A hypothetical service writes cache files beneath /work/cache. Propose a read-only root filesystem plus a dedicated bounded writable mount there. Do not mount the host root or grant privileged mode just because the application failed a write during startup.

tasks.name: Bind scan evidence to deployment
tasks.goal: Avoid scanning one image and running another.
steps: Record scan digest D1, then notice release tag latest now resolves to D2. Expected decision: D1's report does not validate D2. Require identification and appropriate evaluation of the actual deployment digest, with evidence status explicitly pending.

key_terms: Rootless: daemon and containers without host-root execution.
Capability: scoped privileged operation permission.
CVE: identifier for a publicly disclosed vulnerability.
Reachability: whether affected code can participate in relevant execution.
lesson.safety: Use offline reviews only. Never mount the Docker socket, enable privileged mode or test container escapes on a host.
cleanup: Keep the hypothetical finding dispositions; no images, scanners, users or runtime configurations were changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical team runs as a nonroot container user and calls the whole platform rootless and secure. What distinctions matter?
interview_points: Distinguish process identity from daemon host privilege.
Review capabilities, mounts and syscall controls.
Treat scanning as limited evidence, not a guarantee.
Tie findings and provenance to the deployed digest.

containers/container-security-rootless-b.core: Nonroot USER is not rootless daemon operation. Combine least privilege, scoped writes, safe build inputs and current scanning. Triage findings with evidence and evaluate the exact digest deployed rather than a mutable tag.
objectives: Connect scan evidence to deployment identity and runtime policy.
prerequisites: Understand image layers, Linux identities and container mounts.

storyboard.title: A scan report applies to a digest, not a moving tag
storyboard.objective: Preserve the evidence chain from build to runtime.

scenes.title: Evaluate the built artifact
scenes.caption: Findings describe the selected image content.
scenes.narration: The scanner evaluates digest D1, and the team records applicable findings and unresolved risks for that exact artifact.

scenes.title: Tag changes afterward
scenes.caption: Another digest is outside the original scan's evidence.
scenes.narration: A mutable tag moves to a different image. Deploying it would disconnect the scan report from the code that actually runs.

scenes.title: Verify identity and restrictions
scenes.caption: Deploy the evaluated digest with independent runtime controls.
scenes.narration: The deployment selects the evaluated digest and applies nonroot identity, limited privileges and scoped writes, without claiming scanning proves complete safety.

lesson.title: Docker Compose local integration environments
lesson.why: Local integrations should be repeatable without becoming accidental public services or sharing hidden data between projects. Compose describes related containers, but reliable startup still requires explicit networks, health conditions, configuration and cleanup ownership.
lesson.what: Docker Compose defines services, networks and volumes in a project model. Services can discover one another by name on shared networks. Project scoping reduces naming collisions while persistent volumes and published ports require deliberate lifecycle choices.

concepts.name: Service model
concepts.body: A service declares its image or build, environment, networks and other runtime configuration. Compose creates containers from that model. Stable service names are better dependencies than container IPs, which can change during recreation or replacement.

concepts.name: Startup versus readiness
concepts.body: Dependency ordering alone means a dependency starts before another service, not that it can handle requests. Long-form depends_on can use service_healthy with a configured health check. Applications should still handle connection loss and restarts after initial startup.

concepts.name: Local boundaries
concepts.body: Only publish endpoints needed by the developer, explicitly binding host loopback. An API can reach a database over the project network without publishing the database to the host. Use synthetic credentials or nonsecret test configuration, never production environment files.

concepts.name: Project and data lifecycle
concepts.body: Distinct project names scope containers and networks, while declared external resources have separate ownership. Compose down ordinarily removes project containers and networks but not named volumes unless requested. Removing volumes is a data deletion decision, not a harmless universal cleanup option.

e2e: Review the Compose model and resolve intended local configuration without production secrets.
Start project-scoped services with only necessary loopback endpoints published.
Wait for meaningful health conditions and exercise application-to-dependency behavior.
Stop the named project and decide separately whether its synthetic persistent data should be retained.

tasks.name: Draw a minimal project
steps: Offline, define API and database services on one project network. Publish only API host loopback port 8080 to its container port. Expected database reachability is by service name from API, not by exposing a database host port to every interface.

tasks.name: Calculate readiness timing
steps: A database process starts at second zero and becomes ready at second twelve; API starts at second two. Without readiness gating, its first connection may fail for ten seconds. Add a meaningful health condition and bounded application reconnect behavior.

tasks.name: Review configuration without starting
steps: If you already have a synthetic disposable Compose file with no secrets, run `docker compose config --no-interpolate` from its folder. This validates and renders configuration without starting services. Otherwise review the command offline; do not render production environment values into logs.

tasks.name: Plan explicit cleanup
steps: For fictional project lesson-demo, separate container/network removal from named-volume deletion. Record whether test records should persist for the next run. Reject a global prune command and explain why external volumes must not be treated as owned by this demo.

key_terms: Compose project: scoped group of related resources.
Service: declared container workload configuration.
depends_on: Compose dependency relationship.
External volume: storage with lifecycle outside the project.
lesson.safety: Use only an existing synthetic model or paper design. Do not start paid services, expose nonloopback ports or load production secrets.
cleanup: No services are started here; future cleanup must name the exact project and explicitly decide whether its own synthetic volumes may be deleted.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical Compose API fails on startup even though depends_on lists its database. What would you change?
interview_points: Distinguish process start from database readiness.
Use a meaningful health check and supported dependency condition.
Retain bounded reconnect logic for later restarts.
Keep internal database access on the project network.

containers/docker-compose-local-integrat.core: Compose scopes a local integration model, not automatic application readiness. Use stable service names, health-aware startup and reconnect logic. Publish only necessary loopback endpoints, and treat persistent-volume deletion as a separate owned-data decision.
objectives: Design a private local Compose topology.
Explain readiness gating and project-scoped cleanup.
prerequisites: Understand containers, service DNS and persistent volumes.

storyboard.title: The database starts before it is ready
storyboard.objective: Explain Compose startup ordering and application reconnects.

scenes.title: Dependency process starts
scenes.caption: The database still needs initialization time.
scenes.narration: Compose starts the database service, but initialization continues before the database can answer application queries.

scenes.title: API connects too early
scenes.caption: Ordering alone cannot guarantee readiness.
scenes.narration: The API attempts its connection while the database is still starting. A dependency list by itself does not make the connection succeed.

scenes.title: Gate and reconnect
scenes.caption: Use health-aware startup plus bounded runtime recovery.
scenes.narration: A meaningful health condition gates initial startup, and the API retains bounded reconnect behavior for later database restarts or brief connection loss.

lesson.title: Container debugging resource limits and health checks
lesson.why: A restarting container may be failing its process, exhausting a resource or simply reporting unhealthy. These are different signals with different recovery behavior; collecting exact evidence prevents ineffective restart loops and unnecessary privilege escalation.
lesson.what: Container debugging correlates process exits, logs, resource limits and application health. A health check adds a status signal, but restart behavior depends on the runtime or orchestrator. Interpret the actual configured lifecycle policy rather than assuming every unhealthy status triggers recovery.

concepts.name: Exit evidence
concepts.body: Record the exit code, runtime state and recent logs for the exact container instance. A nonzero exit narrows possibilities but is not a complete root cause. Recreated containers may lose useful local evidence, so capture the first failure before repeated replacement.

concepts.name: Memory and CPU limits
concepts.body: Memory pressure can trigger an OOM kill at the workload boundary despite spare host memory. CPU limits can cause throttling rather than termination. Compare demand and cgroup evidence with latency; increasing a limit without understanding growth can postpone a leak rather than solve it.

concepts.name: Health check semantics
concepts.body: A health command reports application-specific status after configured intervals, timeouts and retries. Docker health status alone does not automatically restart an unhealthy but running container. Compose or an orchestrator may use the signal differently; distinguish readiness from liveness policy.

concepts.name: Minimal diagnostic access
concepts.body: Prefer logs, read-only inspection and known application diagnostics before entering a container. Minimal images may lack shells or tools by design. Use approved disposable debugging methods when needed rather than permanently adding broad tools, host mounts or privileged execution.

e2e: Identify the exact failed container and preserve its state and earliest relevant logs.
Separate process exit, unhealthy status and resource-pressure evidence.
Form a specific hypothesis and inspect the application's configured health and restart contracts.
Apply a narrow reviewed correction and verify useful responses under representative bounded load.

tasks.name: Classify three failures
steps: Offline, compare exit 1 with a parse error, a running but unhealthy process and an OOM-marked termination. Investigate configuration, health-command behavior and memory pressure respectively. Do not infer a single universal remedy from the shared symptom that users see failures.

tasks.name: Calculate memory pressure
tasks.goal: Relate working set to a limit.
steps: A hypothetical container limit is 256 MiB; steady demand is 220 MiB and a request adds 60 MiB. Estimated demand becomes 280 MiB, exceeding the limit by 24 MiB. Consider concurrency reduction or memory fixes before merely repeating failed requests.

tasks.name: Interpret a health timeline
steps: A Docker container remains running while three health checks fail. Expected status can become unhealthy, but ordinary Docker health status alone does not promise a restart. Read the actual supervisor policy and distinguish its health reaction from process-exit restart behavior.

tasks.name: Plan safe inspection
tasks.goal: Collect useful evidence without broad access.
steps: For a container you personally own, review the commands `docker logs --tail 50 NAME` and `docker inspect NAME` before use. Inspection can reveal environment secrets, so prefer selected nonsecret fields and never publish raw output. Keep this exercise offline if no owned demo exists.

key_terms: OOM kill: termination under enforced memory exhaustion.
Throttling: delayed CPU execution due to limits.
Health status: result of configured application probes.
Restart policy: rules governing process replacement after lifecycle events.
lesson.safety: Do not inspect unrelated containers or expose environment secrets. No stress tests, privileged debugging or host-control mounts are needed.
cleanup: No containers are started; retain only redacted hypothetical evidence and remove any local diagnostic output containing sensitive values.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical Docker container is unhealthy but never restarts. Is the runtime ignoring its health check?
interview_points: Health status and restart triggers are different mechanisms.
Inspect the actual restart or orchestrator policy.
Check the health command's meaning and timeout.
Preserve logs and resource evidence before changing lifecycle behavior.

containers/container-debugging-resource-.core: Separate process exit, health status and resource pressure. CPU throttling differs from OOM termination. Docker health status alone does not restart a running container; inspect actual supervisor policy and collect minimal redacted evidence.
objectives: Explain resource limits and health-dependent lifecycle behavior.
prerequisites: Understand container processes, limits and logs.

storyboard.title: Unhealthy does not necessarily mean restarted
storyboard.objective: Separate health observations from lifecycle policy.

scenes.title: Process remains running
scenes.caption: Health checks observe application behavior separately.
scenes.narration: The container's main process runs while a configured health command tests a specific application condition at regular intervals.

scenes.title: Health fails repeatedly
scenes.caption: An unhealthy status is not itself a universal restart trigger.
scenes.narration: Repeated probe failures mark the container unhealthy. The running process may remain because its restart policy reacts to process exit instead.

scenes.title: Inspect the policy and cause
scenes.caption: Diagnose the probe and actual supervisor contract.
scenes.narration: The operator reviews health meaning, resource evidence and lifecycle policy, then fixes the cause rather than assuming status must automatically force replacement.
